title: Bruised knee: safe early care and deciding when to get checked
intro: A direct blow or fall can bruise the soft tissues around the knee, causing tenderness, swelling and skin colour changes. A bruise may be minor, but the same incident can also injure bone, cartilage or ligaments. The amount of visible bruising does not show the whole injury. This guide concerns a suspected knee contusion; severe symptoms or loss of function need assessment before assuming simple home care is enough.

sections.heading: Check for signs of a more serious injury
paragraphs: Seek prompt assessment if you cannot bear weight or move the knee, swelling is substantial or rapidly increasing, the joint locks or gives way, or its shape has changed. An open deep wound also needs assessment. A cold, pale or numb foot, major deformity or severe rapidly worsening pain requires emergency help. Fever with a hot painful knee needs urgent review for possible infection. Do not repeatedly test the joint by jumping or forcing it to bend, and do not let a small surface bruise reassure you after a major impact.

sections.heading: Describe the injury and what changed afterwards
paragraphs: Explain whether you fell directly onto the knee, hit an object or also twisted it. Tell the clinician when swelling appeared, whether you heard a pop and what walking or straightening is like. Mention earlier knee problems, joint replacement, bleeding disorders and blood-thinning medicines. Examination helps decide whether an X-ray or other assessment is needed; not every bruise requires a scan. Persistent focal bone pain or an unexpected recovery pattern should be reassessed rather than explained solely by the first label of bruise.

sections.heading: Protect the knee and use cold safely
paragraphs: If the injury is suitable for home care, reduce activities that aggravate pain and avoid kneeling on the injured area. A cold pack wrapped in cloth can ease discomfort and swelling; protect the skin and do not leave it on until the area becomes painfully cold or numb. Elevating the leg when resting may help. If using a support or compression, ask how to fit it and remove it if it causes numbness, increasing pain or colour change. Do not aggressively massage a fresh swelling or try to drain it yourself.

sections.heading: Balance relief with a gradual return to movement
paragraphs: Ask a pharmacist or clinician which pain medicine is suitable with your health and other treatments, especially with anticoagulants, kidney disease or pregnancy. More medicine does not make it safe to play through pain. Once serious injury has been excluded, gentle movement within comfort and gradually increasing activity can help avoid prolonged stiffness. Follow specific advice if a clinician recommends a brace or restrictions. Return to demanding work or sport depends on function, pain, swelling and the task, not just whether the bruise has faded.

sections.heading: Review recovery and new warning signs
paragraphs: Bruise colour may change while healing, but the overall direction should be towards less pain and better function. Seek reassessment if pain or swelling worsens, improvement does not occur as expected, or walking remains difficult. Report spreading warmth, redness, fever or wound discharge. New calf swelling or pain should not be assumed to come from the bruise; urgent assessment may be needed for another cause. Chest pain or breathlessness with leg symptoms requires emergency help. Recurrent unexplained bruising also deserves advice, particularly after a medicine change.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a small bruise with poor function
examples.text: After a fall, someone sees only a small mark but cannot put weight on the leg. They seek assessment rather than judging the injury by colour alone. They explain the impact and any blood-thinning treatment instead of repeatedly trying to run on it.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: returning to activity
examples.text: A person with an assessed uncomplicated bruise can walk comfortably but kneeling still hurts. They adjust work tasks and gradually increase movement. They arrange review if swelling grows instead of using extra painkillers to force a return to the same pressure.

questions: Does the injury fit a simple bruise, or do the examination and symptoms suggest bone or joint damage?
Which pain relief, support and movement are suitable for me?
What recovery pattern should I expect, and which changes require earlier assessment?
